laterality.sharedOverview: Middle-back pain refers to the thoracic region between the neck and lower back. It may come from muscle strain, posture, rib or costovertebral joint dysfunction, degenerative changes, disc problems, osteoarthritis, spinal stenosis, injury, rib fracture, shingles, or other musculoskeletal causes. Pain in this region can also sometimes be referred from internal organs, including the lungs, kidneys, stomach, pancreas, liver, gallbladder, or spleen depending on side and location. Possible reflective themes vary by side: this area can invite exploration of old burdens, guilt, unsupported responsibility, and carrying unresolved emotional weight from the past. These are reflection themes only and are not presented as medical causes of middle-back pain.
laterality.sharedSafetyNote: Do not treat middle-back pain as usually emotional. Seek medical evaluation for major trauma, chest pain or pressure, significant shortness of breath, fever, unexplained weight loss, severe pain with breathing or coughing, progressive weakness or numbness, new neurologic symptoms, or severe flank/abdominal symptoms. Side-specific organ referral is possible but never automatic: left-sided pain does not prove a stomach/pancreas/spleen source, and right-sided pain does not prove a liver/gallbladder source.

laterality.sharedOverview: Upper-back pain can arise from muscles, joints, ribs, the cervical or upper thoracic spine, nerves, posture, repetitive strain, or injury. Common possibilities include trapezius, levator scapulae, or rhomboid strain or overuse; forward-head posture; prolonged computer or phone use; cervical radiculopathy; disc or degenerative changes; osteoarthritis; rib or scapular-region problems; and other musculoskeletal conditions. Pain in the upper back or shoulder-blade region can also sometimes be referred from internal organs or the chest. Possible reflective themes vary by side: this area can invite exploration of responsibility, caretaking, emotional burden, and the sense of holding everything together while feeling unsupported. These are reflection themes only and are not presented as medical causes of upper-back pain.
laterality.sharedSafetyNote: Do not treat upper-back pain as usually emotional or postural. Seek prompt medical evaluation for chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw; new weakness; new numbness; progressive neurologic symptoms; major trauma; fever; unexplained severe pain; significant breathing-related pain; or other red-flag symptoms. Left-sided cardiac referral is possible but never automatic, and right-sided pain does not automatically indicate a gallbladder, liver, or lung source.

hero.primaryPattern: Upper-back pain can come from trapezius, levator scapulae, or rhomboid strain; forward-head posture; prolonged screen use; cervical radiculopathy; disc or degenerative changes; osteoarthritis; rib or scapular-region problems; or referred pain from the chest or internal organs. hero.safetyPreview: Emergency/urgent signs include chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, arm/jaw pain, sweating, nausea, fever, unexplained weight loss, weakness/numbness, trauma, significant breathing pain, or worsening neurologic symptoms.

biologyPathway.title: Mechanical Load
biologyPathway.detail: Upper-back pain can arise from trapezius, levator scapulae, or rhomboid strain or overuse, posture, rib or costovertebral dysfunction, repetitive movement, disc problems, osteoarthritis, or injury.

biologyPathway.title: Nerve Pathway
biologyPathway.detail: Pain with numbness, weakness, tingling, or radiating symptoms can involve nerve irritation or compression, including cervical radiculopathy.

biologyPathway.title: Referred Pain
biologyPathway.detail: Upper-back or shoulder-blade pain can sometimes be referred from internal organs or the chest, including cardiac, lung, gallbladder, liver, or other structures depending on side, location, and associated symptoms. Side alone does not confirm an organ source.

biologyPathway.title: Stress and Guarding
biologyPathway.detail: Stress may influence muscle tension, posture, pain perception, sleep, and guarding, which can worsen pain cycles. This is not a single-cause explanation and does not replace evaluation of physical causes.

clinical.label: Strictly Medical
clinical.title: Upper Back Problems: Mechanical, Nerve, Referred & Stress-Tension Screen

sections.heading: Stage 1 — Locate and Screen
body: Upper-back pain should be screened by location, side, onset, severity, trauma, radiation, neurologic symptoms, chest/breathing symptoms, fever, and medical history.
Side-specific symbolism is optional. Side-specific organ referral is possible but never automatic, because referred pain has many sources.

sections.heading: Stage 2 — Common Physical Causes
body: Upper-back pain may come from trapezius, levator scapulae, or rhomboid strain or overuse; forward-head posture; prolonged screen or desk use; cervical radiculopathy; disc or degenerative changes; osteoarthritis; rib or scapular-region problems; injury; or other musculoskeletal conditions.
Pain can also be referred from the chest or internal organs, so side, location, and associated symptoms matter.

sections.heading: Stage 3 — Symbolic Layer
body: Symbolically, this area may invite exploration of responsibility, caretaking, emotional burden, and the sense of holding everything together while feeling unsupported. Left-sided symptoms may point toward grief and sorrow; right-sided symptoms may point toward action, expression, and responsibility.
This is a reflection layer, not a diagnosis and not a claim of cause.

sections.heading: Stage 4 — Care Direction
body: Care may include movement modification, heat/ice, gentle mobility, physical therapy, posture/ergonomic changes, medical evaluation, imaging when indicated, medication when appropriate, or emergency care for red flags.
The goal is to treat the body and learn from the pattern without making either one carry the whole circus.

witty.label: Comedic & Witty
witty.title: The Overloaded Backpack
paragraphs: Your upper back is the coat rack, backpack frame, and emergency storage shelf of the torso.
Sometimes the problem is posture, a strained muscle, irritated nerve, joint, rib, lung, or referred pain from somewhere less poetic.
Symbolically, though, it is a suspiciously believable place to notice how many other people's backpacks you volunteered to carry.
First check danger signs. Then check mechanics. Then check the life pattern.
The symbolism can help you listen. The red flags tell you when listening needs a doctor.
Repack the backpack safely or keep letting one strap hold the entire human condition. Your choice.

brutal.label: Brutally Honest
brutal.title: The Atlas Complex Reality Check
paragraphs: You may have Upper Back Problems. You may also notice themes of responsibility, caretaking, emotional burden, and holding everything together while feeling unsupported.
Medical first: trauma, neurologic changes, fever, chest/breathing symptoms, unexplained weight loss, or severe pain changes the game.
The hard truth: your body may be telling you something about load, movement, posture, fear, grief, obligation, or support.
The other hard truth: sometimes it is a trapezius strain, cervical disc, rib dysfunction, lung, heart, gallbladder, liver, or other physical issue. The metaphor does not get to outrank biology.

Before deciding your shoulder blades are carrying ancestral responsibility for the entire bloodline, check whether you have spent fourteen hours hunched over a screen like a gargoyle with Wi-Fi. Then check the actual red flags. After anatomy gets its turn, you can investigate why you keep volunteering to manage everyone else's emotional luggage.
Repack the backpack safely or keep letting one strap hold the entire human condition. Your choice.

influenceLayers.title: Atlas Complex
paragraphs: In symbolic body mapping, the upper back can symbolize holding up the world, carrying responsibility, and shouldering burdens for others.
This is optional reflection, not medical proof.

influenceLayers.title: Support Beam
paragraphs: The upper back can be imagined as a support beam carrying weight—both physical and emotional.
This is a reflection layer, not a diagnosis.

influenceLayers.title: Left Side — Grief and Sorrow
paragraphs: Left-sided upper-back patterns may invite reflection on grief, sorrow, caretaking, and emotional burden.
This is a reflection layer, not a diagnosis.

influenceLayers.title: Right Side — Action and Expression
paragraphs: Right-sided upper-back patterns may invite reflection on action, expression, responsibility, and performance pressure.
This is a reflection layer, not a diagnosis.

influenceLayers.title: Set Down / Move Forward
paragraphs: The reset is not pretending pain is emotional.
It is checking safety, supporting tissue, and asking what the body no longer wants to carry.

reset.title: Upper Back Reset & Load Release
steps: Screen red flags first: chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, arm/jaw pain, sweating, nausea, faintness, fever, unexplained weight loss, weakness/numbness, trauma, severe breathing pain, or worsening neurologic symptoms.
If red flags are present, seek medical care urgently.
If safe, sit supported or lie on your back with knees bent.
Breathe in for 4 seconds and exhale for 8 seconds while softening the upper back and shoulder blades.
Ask: what physical load needs adjustment, and what emotional load needs to be set down or shared?

naturalSupport.title: Supportive Care
naturalSupport.disclaimer: Supportive care is not a cure. Upper-back pain may require medical evaluation, physical therapy, imaging, medication, or emergency care depending on symptoms.

items.label: Gentle movement
items.detail: Short walks and gentle mobility may help many non-emergency back pain patterns.

items.label: Heat or ice
items.detail: Heat or ice may reduce discomfort depending on the situation and preference.

items.label: Physical therapy
items.detail: PT can assess upper-back mobility, posture, shoulder-blade mechanics, nerve signs, and movement patterns.

items.label: Medical evaluation
items.detail: Needed for red flags, persistent pain, neurologic symptoms, referred pain concerns, or worsening function.

avoid: Do not ignore chest pain, shortness of breath, arm/jaw pain, sweating, nausea, fever, saddle numbness, new weakness/numbness, trauma, significant breathing pain, or unexplained severe pain.
Do not force stretches through sharp, worsening, radiating, or neurologic pain.

brutalActions: Set down one emotional load that is not yours.

critical_alerts: Back pain after major trauma, fall, accident, or injury
New weakness, numbness, tingling, pain down arm, or saddle numbness, or bowel/bladder changes
Fever, chills, infection concern, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, steroid use, osteoporosis, or immune suppression
Chest pain or pressure, or significant shortness of breath
Sweating, nausea, faintness, or left upper-back pain with cardiac symptoms
Sweating, nausea, faintness, jaw/arm pain, or pain spreading from chest
Significant breathing-related pain
Right upper-back/shoulder pain with right upper abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, jaundice, or fatty-meal trigger may need gallbladder/liver evaluation
seek_immediate_care_if: Pain follows trauma, comes with chest symptoms, shortness of breath, arm/jaw pain, sweating, nausea, faintness, new weakness/numbness, saddle numbness, bowel/bladder changes, severe breathing pain, fever/infection signs, or severe sudden worsening
Left upper-back pain with chest pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, jaw/arm pain, or exertional symptoms may be cardiac and needs urgent care
schedule_care_if: Pain persists beyond a week or two, worsens, limits function, radiates, recurs, appears after age 50, or has concerning medical history
medical_safety.self_care_allowed_if: Gentle movement, posture changes, heat/ice, rest from aggravating activity, and reflection may support mild non-emergency back pain. Prolonged bed rest is usually not recommended for uncomplicated back pain.
medical_safety.do_not_ignore: Upper-back pain can be mechanical, nerve-related, rib-related, organ-referred, infection-related, cancer-related, or cardiac/lung-related depending on location and symptoms. Red flags change the plan.
medical_safety.disclaimer: This app is for education and self-reflection only. It does not diagnose, treat, prevent, or cure back pain.
